title: Engineering Specifications & Requirements
summary: Turning product needs into measurable, testable engineering specifications with requirement decomposition, spec sheets, and QFD prioritization.

infobox.title: Engineering Specifications
infobox.siUnits: Mixed: mm, N, °C, W, m/s per parameter

sections.heading: Why Specifications Matter
sections.content:
A specification is a **measurable, unambiguous technical contract** between design intent and the rest of the product lifecycle — manufacturing, inspection, suppliers, and testing. Without specifications, requirements live in someone's head, and every downstream decision (tolerance, tooling, test plan) becomes a guess that gets discovered at the worst possible time: in production.

The rule of thumb: **if you cannot write the acceptance criterion for a requirement, you do not have a requirement — you have an opinion.** A spec must state the parameter, the unit, the numerical limit or band, the condition under which it applies, and the method used to verify it.

sections.heading: From Function to Number
sections.content:
Product development starts with **customer/functional requirements (CR)** — qualitative statements of what the product must do — and ends with **engineering specifications (SR)** — quantitative statements that can be measured.

Example decomposition for a hand crank assembly:

| Customer/functional requirement | Engineering specification |
|---|---|
| The crank must not wobble | Shaft runout ≤ 0.05 mm at bearing seat, per ASME B89 |
| It must be easy to turn | Operating torque ≤ 2.0 N·m at 20 °C |
| It must survive daily use | 50 000 cycles, load 150 N, no failure per DVP-R |

Each functional requirement should map to **at least one** engineering specification, and every specification should trace back to a requirement. This two-way traceability is the basis of requirements management in formal product development.

sections.heading: Anatomy of a Specification Sheet
sections.content:
A mature spec sheet records these fields for each parameter:

- **Parameter** — what is controlled (e.g. flatness, pull-out force).
- **Nominal value and tolerance band** — written as $X \pm t$ or as a limit (min/max).
- **Unit** — never omit; a missing unit has caused real spacecraft failures.
- **Condition** — environmental or state context (temperature, humidity, load case, orientation).
- **Acceptance method** — the instrument and procedure: CMM, gauge, torque wrench, test rig.
- **Reference standard** — ISO, ASME, ASTM, or internal test method number.
- **Revision and owner** — who may change it and when it was last reviewed.

Write the band to be **achievable by the chosen process** — a specification is not a wish; it is a commitment the process must hold. Linking each line to process capability (see [[quality-control-and-spc|SPC]] and [[iso-fits-and-surface-finish|ISO fits]]) keeps specs realistic.

sections.heading: QFD & the House of Quality
sections.content:
When requirements multiply, **Quality Function Deployment (QFD)** prioritizes them so engineering effort follows customer value. The House of Quality matrix rows are customer requirements, columns are engineering specifications, and each cell holds a relationship rating $r_{ij}$ (e.g. 1 = weak, 3 = medium, 9 = strong).

The **importance weight** of each engineering specification is:

$$W_j = \sum_i r_{ij} \cdot w_i$$

where $w_i$ is the customer importance of requirement $i$. The roof of the house captures trade-offs between specifications (improving one may worsen another — e.g. strength vs mass) — these conflicts are exactly the decisions design reviews must resolve deliberately.

sections.heading: Verification & the DVP
sections.content:
A specification is only as good as its verification. The **Design Verification Plan & Report (DVP-R)** lists each critical specification with:

1. **Item** — the specification or feature under test.
2. **Test method** — rig, procedure, standard, sample size.
3. **Conditions** — load, temperature, cycles, media.
4. **Acceptance criteria** — the spec values from the sheet.
5. **Result & status** — pass/fail with evidence, and who signed it.

Early prototypes are verified against **critical specifications first** (see [[prototype-testing-and-validation|prototype testing]]); production then keeps those same specs alive through SPC and incoming inspection ([[metrology-and-inspection|metrology]]). A spec that is never verified should be deleted — it adds cost without value.

sections.heading: Common Specification Failures
sections.content:
Real projects fail specifications in a handful of repeatable ways:

- **Vague adjectives** — "smooth surface", "strong enough" — always translate to numbers (Ra 1.6 µm, safety factor 2).
- **Mixed target and limit** — decide per parameter: is $X \pm t$ a target with tolerance, or a one-sided limit (max 2 N·m)?
- **Missing units or conditions** — the spec must be valid at a stated temperature, humidity, and load case.
- **Over-constraining** — every extra tolerance costs money; specify only features that affect function or assembly (see [[tolerance-stack-up-analysis|tolerance stacks]]).
- **No verification method** — if it cannot be measured, it cannot be bought or released.

Review the spec sheet at every design gate, and let manufacturing challenge any band that exceeds demonstrated capability before tooling is cut.

keyTakeaways: A specification must be measurable, unambiguous, and tied to a verification method.
Trace every engineering specification back to a customer/functional requirement.
Use QFD importance weights W_j = sum of r_ij × w_i to prioritize specifications.
Unverifiable or unachievable specifications are worse than none — delete or renegotiate them.
